items.headline: XIAOMI Q2: revenue -6.1%, adjusted profit -42.6%, and NO interim dividend — the reaction is this morning's session
items.summary: Read in full from Xiaomi's own results presentation, not a wire summary. GROUP: revenue RMB108.9bn (-6.1% y/y, +9.9% q/q); gross margin 19.8% against 22.5% a year earlier; adjusted net profit RMB6.2bn with an adjusted margin of 5.7% against 9.3%. IFRS profit RMB9.463bn (-20.3%); H1 revenue RMB208.1bn (-8.4%). SEGMENTS: Smartphone x AIoT RMB84.0bn at 20.0% gross margin; smartphones alone RMB42.1bn at just 8.5% gross margin, which the deck attributes verbatim to 'substantial increased price of key components'; IoT RMB31.3bn at 20.1%; internet services RMB9.0bn. Shipments 31.2m units, DOWN 26.3% y/y, 11.5% global share, No.3 for a 24th straight quarter. But ASP hit a record RMB1,351, +25.9% y/y, and the China premium mix (>=RMB3,000) rose 4.5ppt to 32.1% — so the unit collapse is partly deliberate mix shift. R&D RMB9.2bn (+18.9%). THE DIVIDEND, which was a genuine open question: NO dividend was declared. The 17 July board notice said 'an interim dividend, if any', so it could not be assumed either way; the corporate-actions record for 1810 confirms 'no second interim dividend', following no first interim in May and no final in March. AGAINST THE ONE DATED PREVIEW I could verify (UOB Kay Hian, 3 Aug, HOLD, target cut to HK$31.50): revenue beat by 5.7% and adjusted profit beat by 5.7%, while gross margin missed by 1.2ppt. TWO CLAIMS REMOVED as unverifiable: an operating profit figure of RMB10.87bn appears on none of the pages opened, including the company's own deck.
items.actionable: Your 26,662 shares rose 1.16% Tuesday BEFORE the numbers — the release landed after the HK close, so the entire reaction sits in this morning's 09:30 session. Two forces pull against each other: adjusted profit beat the one verifiable preview by 5.7%, but a -42.6% y/y collapse and the confirmed absence of a dividend remove a catalyst some holders were positioned for after the 'if any' language. The number to track is the 8.5% smartphone gross margin, not headline revenue — that is where the component-cost squeeze shows up.

items.headline: Xiaomi's EV arm lost RMB2.6bn at the operating line — a loss that WIDENED roughly 8x year-on-year, and deliveries fell sequentially
items.summary: CORRECTED DURING VERIFICATION, because the obvious read was wrong in a way that mattered. Smart EV, AI and other new initiatives: revenue RMB24.9bn (+17.1% y/y), EV sales RMB23.9bn (+15.9%). Deliveries 104,199, up 28.2% y/y but DOWN sequentially from 108,796 in Q1 2026 and 145,115 in Q4 2025. Segment gross margin 19.2% against 26.4%, which the company attributes to a lower SU7 Ultra mix, higher key-component prices and rising AI costs. Segment operating loss RMB2.6bn. THE REFUTATION: the first draft said this reversed a RMB0.3bn operating PROFIT a year earlier. It did not — Q2 2025 was itself a RMB0.3bn LOSS that had been narrowing. So the correct read is a loss that widened roughly eightfold year-on-year while improving on Q1's RMB3.1bn. THE DELIVERY ARITHMETIC, done from company figures only: H1 was 212,995 units, leaving 337,005 against the 550,000 full-year target — about 56,200 per month for the rest of the year, against a Q2 run-rate near 34,700. The CFO explicitly reaffirmed the 550,000 target. Per-vehicle ASP RMB229,312, -9.6% y/y on the weaker Ultra mix. The first extended-range SUV, the SkyNomad series, launches in September at RMB299,900 and RMB259,900 pre-sale. On the call, management said memory-cost inflation persists into Q4 but at a slower pace and that the phone business has 'already approached the end of its most difficult period'. REMOVED: a claim that SkyNomad pre-orders were 'significantly exceeding expectations' appears on none of the pages opened.
items.actionable: This is the most negative datapoint in the release, but for the right reason: the segment did not swing from profit to loss, it deepened an existing loss eightfold while improving on Q1. The gap to the reaffirmed 550,000 target is the thing to watch — 56,200 a month needed against a 34,700 run-rate, with September's SkyNomad launch as the swing factor. The memory-cost commentary reads across to the whole HK handset and component complex, not just to your position.

items.headline: SILVER'S 2x UNDERPERFORMANCE WAS A BOND ROUT, NOT A SILVER STORY — and the dollar was flat
items.summary: Silver fell 3.58% and gold 1.71% (both measured on the ETFs, which cannot roll — see the method note below). Silver underperformed gold by more than 2x and the ratio widened again. THE DRIVER WAS THE LONG END, not anything silver-specific: no inventory event, no squeeze unwind, no industrial-demand news could be found on any dated page. The dollar was FLAT on the session, which rules out the usual mechanical explanation. What moved was global duration — the US 30-year touched 5.32% intraday, its highest since 2007, and Japan's 10-year JGB hit 2.945%, its highest since SEPTEMBER 1996. A non-yielding levered asset is the purest expression of a real-rate shock, which is why silver took roughly double gold's hit. IMPORTANT NUANCE FROM VERIFICATION: the long end did NOT finish higher. After the 5.32% intraday print the 30-year CLOSED down 2bp at 5.29%, and the 10-year eased to around 4.70% from 4.73%. So Tuesday was equity and metals de-risking at an already-elevated level of rates, not a fresh long-end shock on the day.
items.actionable: At 1.6x, Tuesday cost roughly 5.7% on the levered silver leg — the worst single session of the run. The read that matters: this was duration, not silver. That means it does not resolve on a silver catalyst; it resolves on the long end, and the FOMC minutes land Thursday 02:00 SGT. Note the small consolation that the 30-year actually closed lower on the day, so the selling was positioning rather than a fresh rates shock.

items.headline: DATA FLAG: Barrick fell 7.82% with NO catalyst anywhere in the public record — reported honestly rather than explained away
items.summary: Barrick closed 41.84, down 7.82%, against a sector that fell 3.2%. AN INDEPENDENT SEARCH FOUND NO COMPANY NEWS DATED TUESDAY 18 AUGUST. Every verifiable catalyst is a week old: Q2 results and the US$1.95bn Newmont/Nevada Gold Mines settlement on 10 August, on which the stock already fell 6.41% that day on an adjusted EPS miss ($0.82 against $0.84) and gold cash costs of $1,993/oz against $1,654 a year earlier; and a BofA target cut to $54 from $56 on 11 August, citing a $2.8bn NAV reduction on Fourmile. Neither is Tuesday. THE PRICE ITSELF CHECKS OUT, which is why it is published: volume was 402,704 against a 248k-392k recent run-rate — entirely normal, not a thin-print artifact — and the intraday range is real, opening 44.75, high 44.77, low 41.78. So the stock gapped down about 1.4% at the open and then collapsed through the session. A live wire quoting Barrick 'down about 1.1%' was reading that early gap, not the day. A claim that institutional investors were revolting over ~15% dilution was STRUCK: the cited page returns HTTP 403 and none of it could be verified.
items.actionable: A 7.8% single-day move on normal volume with no identifiable cause is worth more of your attention than a move with an obvious one — it usually means either a large holder is selling or something is known to the market that is not yet in the record. Treat the position accordingly and watch for a filing or a downgrade in the next day or two. I would rather tell you the cause is unknown than supply a plausible-sounding one.

items.headline: The long end went global: US 30Y touched 5.32%, a post-2007 high, and Japan's 10Y hit 2.945% — its highest since September 1996
items.summary: A genuinely global duration move rather than a US story. The US 10-year printed 4.748% at one point, its highest since January 2025, and the 30-year 5.32-5.33%, a 19-year high. Japan's 10-year JGB reached 2.945%, a level not seen since September 1996, on Bank of Japan September hike expectations and Middle East risk. The attribution is fiscal and supply-driven rather than growth-driven: investors 'increasingly twitchy about inflation, public finances, and policymakers' ability — or willingness — to get them under control', compounded by corporate crowding-out, with total issuance near $1.7 trillion year-to-date, up about 27% year on year. A specific and striking figure: technology companies have sold roughly $192bn of bonds through late July against $61bn five years ago, as AI capital spending moves onto the bond market. CORRECTIONS APPLIED: a CNBC page cited for the 5.33% headline returns HTTP 403 and was struck; the figures above come from pages that opened. And the day did NOT end higher — the 30-year closed down 2bp at 5.29%. September Fed pricing did NOT move on any of this, holding at 35.3% for a hike.
items.actionable: This is the mechanism behind both the silver drop and the REIT pressure, and it is now visibly structural rather than cyclical: AI capex is being funded in the bond market, and that supply is crowding out duration globally. It will not resolve on a soft inflation print, which is exactly what the past week demonstrated. For the Singapore REIT sleeve this is the binding constraint; for levered silver it is the recurring drawdown risk.

items.headline: Tuesday's US data was soft and disinflationary — and long yields rose anyway. Housing starts collapsed 12.4% while permits BEAT
items.summary: Housing starts fell 12.4% to 1.239m annualised against a 1.350m consensus — a sharp miss. But building permits, the forward-looking series, BEAT at 1.443m. That divergence matters: starts reflect what builders are finishing under current financing costs, permits what they intend. The rest of Tuesday's data was soft-side too. Yet the long end rose through the session regardless, which is the same pattern as last week's in-line CPI and soft PPI producing zero net duration relief. The market is not trading US growth data right now; it is trading supply and fiscal credibility. September Fed pricing was unmoved at 35.3% for a hike.
items.actionable: Three consecutive soft US prints have now failed to rally duration. Stop reading soft data as a REIT or metals catalyst — under a supply-driven long end it simply is not one. The housing starts/permits split is worth watching as a leading indicator: if permits roll over too, that is a genuine growth signal rather than a financing-cost artifact.

items.headline: Equities sorted by leverage and duration, not by sector: PHLX semis fell as much as 5%, Intel -6%, Micron -5%
items.summary: S&P 7,691.76 (-0.69%), Nasdaq 26,289.71 (-1.33%), Dow 53,343.40 (-0.22%), Russell 3,017.89 (-1.30%), VIX 15.84 (+4.28%). The internals are the story: the PHLX Semiconductor Index dropped as much as 5% intraday, on track for its worst day in over two weeks, with Intel -6%, Micron -5%, Sandisk -6% and SK Hynix -6%. The Dow's relative resilience against the Nasdaq and Russell tells you this sorted by duration and leverage rather than by sector — long-duration growth and small caps were hit, defensives were not. A live blog attributed the fall to tech selling plus elevated oil and government bond yields. Note the timing: after last week's memory melt-up, this is the first meaningful reversal in the AI-hardware complex.
items.actionable: The semiconductor reversal is the read-across worth carrying into this morning's HK open — SMIC has been the book's best performer on exactly this theme, and it rose 0.93% on Tuesday before the US semis broke. A 5% PHLX drawdown is a headwind to that trade, though SMIC's driver is domestic pricing power rather than US AI demand, which has decoupled the two before.

items.headline: Energy rose on Iran/Hormuz supply risk — and the Ukrainian-drone explanation circulating for it was refuted
items.summary: XLE rose 1.76% and USO 0.28% on a day equities fell and metals were hit — the only major sleeve that gained. The driver is Iran and Hormuz supply risk, following Monday's formal expiry of the June US-Iran memorandum, Trump's refusal to extend it, and Tehran's signalled 'fully offensive' posture with a several-week ultimatum. REFUTED DURING VERIFICATION: an explanation attributing Tuesday's move to Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian infrastructure could not be substantiated on any dated page and was struck, along with a '$100 oil' price target that appeared only in unsourced commentary. METHOD NOTE, and it applies to every commodity figure in this edition: the futures series on this desk's feed was found to be unreliable — gold front-month returned daily volumes in the hundreds, and Brent and WTI reported identical volumes on two different sessions. All metals and energy percentages here come from ETF proxies, which cannot roll and trade millions of shares daily.
items.actionable: Energy equities outperforming crude itself (XLE +1.76% against USO +0.28%) says the market is pricing sustained higher prices into earnings rather than a spot spike. That is a more durable signal than a one-day crude move. The sleeve remains the natural hedge against the very inflation impulse that is hurting your levered silver through the long end.

items.headline: Asia held up: Hang Seng +0.07% to 25,471.15 while Hang Seng Tech fell 0.90%; STI slipped to 5,701.40
items.summary: Hang Seng closed 25,471.15, up 0.07% — essentially flat, but a second consecutive gain after last week's four-session losing streak. Hang Seng Tech diverged, falling 0.90% to 4,739.18, so the index was carried by non-tech constituents. STI closed 5,701.40. Within the book: Tencent -0.90%, with Mizuho cutting its target price to HK$560 on doubts about the return profile of its AI spending — consistent with the free-cash-flow question raised by its own Q2, where capex rose 176% and FCF went negative for the first time since 2005. SMIC rose 0.93%, holding its post-earnings gains. Xiaomi rose 1.16%, but that was BEFORE its results landed after the close.
items.actionable: The Mizuho note crystallises the Tencent question into a target: the market is no longer arguing about demand, it is arguing about what the AI capex earns. That is the same debate now attached to the long end globally, and it is why your HK tech and your REIT sleeve are quietly exposed to the same variable. SMIC holding its gains through a soft tech tape is the more encouraging signal in the sleeve.

items.headline: SINGAPORE: DBS -1.51% and OCBC -1.90% — and OCBC's is a genuine decline this time, the dividend came off on Monday
items.summary: DBS closed 75.72 (-1.51%) and OCBC 30.95 (-1.90%). IMPORTANT DISTINCTION FROM YESTERDAY: OCBC's 47-cent dividend went ex on MONDAY 17 August, so Monday's headline -0.76% was actually a 0.73% gain once adjusted. Tuesday's -1.90% has no such explanation — it is a real decline, and the two must not be conflated. The same applies to DBS, whose S$0.81 came off on Friday 14 August. Elsewhere: Singtel 4.44 (-0.45%), UOL 9.19 (-0.11%), City Developments 8.10 (+0.25%), MPACT 1.26 (-0.79%). Keppel REIT, Mapletree Logistics and Mapletree Industrial all printed unchanged — normal on SGX, where one tick is 0.5-0.85% on these names.
items.actionable: Both banks fell on a day the global long end sat near post-2007 highs, which is the wrong direction for the usual 'banks like higher rates' reflex — it suggests the market is now reading the long end as a growth and credit risk rather than a margin tailwind. Worth noting the mechanical adjustments are behind you now: DBS pays 25 August, OCBC 28 August, and from here both lines move on fundamentals only.

items.headline: CORRECTION TO YESTERDAY'S BRIEF: gold did NOT break out on Monday. Four figures I published were wrong
items.summary: Yesterday this brief said 'gold broke out and HELD it — new high 4,486.50, closed 4,479.50 (+2.26%), clearing the prior 4,445 peak'. That was wrong. Re-reading the same Monday bar the next morning returned 4,417.80, high 4,428.50, +0.85% — and Monday's high therefore never cleared the 13 August peak. It was another lower high, the opposite of what was reported. THE CAUSE: a futures contract rolled underneath the symbol. Git history proves the change — the bar carried volume 4,739 when published and 673 the next morning. The clean control is GLD, which cannot roll: it rose 1.00% on Monday, agreeing with the revised figure and refuting the published one. THREE OTHER MONDAY FIGURES WERE WRONG THE SAME WAY: Brent 91.11 should have been 90.87 (volume 90 against 29,003 on the real contract), WTI 84.95 should have been 84.50 (1,230 against 192,132), and silver's bar carried volume ZERO. A Brent front-month bar with 90 contracts of volume was never plausible and was not checked. FIXES NOW IN PLACE: a revision detector that diffs every historical bar against the prior run and flags any closed session whose price moves; a thin-bar gate for implausible volumes; trust flags routing metals and energy to ETF proxies; and a validator that now refuses to reconcile against a series the system distrusts. The revision detector itself had a bug found by testing it against this very event — it wrote the file before reading the 'previous' run, so it was diffing today against itself.
items.actionable: The practical consequence: gold has now failed at its highs FOUR consecutive sessions, not three-then-a-breakout. That is a materially more cautious picture for the metals sleeve than yesterday's brief implied, and it is consistent with Tuesday's sharp reversal. Every metals and energy percentage in today's edition comes from ETF proxies rather than futures.

items.headline: TONIGHT: FOMC minutes at 02:00 SGT Thursday — covering the meeting where THREE officials voted for a hike
items.summary: The minutes of the 29 July FOMC land Thursday 20 August 02:00 SGT (Wednesday 19 August 14:00 ET). Confirmed against the calendar feed. They cover the meeting at which Hammack, Kashkari and Logan all dissented in favour of a 25bp INCREASE — the reason there is no cut anywhere in the September distribution, which currently prices 35.3% for a hike and 64.7% for a hold. WHAT TO READ FOR: how close the majority came to joining the three dissenters, and whether September was described as live. THE STALENESS CAVEAT IS REAL AND IMPORTANT: these minutes predate the soft CPI, the soft PPI, the retail-sales miss and the US-Iran MOU expiry. They may well read hawkish relative to where pricing actually sits now, and a hawkish-sounding document about a stale information set is exactly the kind of thing that moves a levered position for the wrong reason. Also this week: China's 1-year and 5-year Loan Prime Rates on Thursday 09:00 SGT, both consensus unchanged at 3.00% and 3.50%.
items.actionable: The asymmetry matters for the levered silver leg. Given the long end is already at post-2007 highs and September prices a 35% hike, a hawkish-reading set of minutes has more room to hurt than a dovish one has to help. Check margin headroom before 02:00 SGT rather than after — the same discipline that applied before CPI.
